**Scoping only, started 2026-09-11, revised 2026-09-12. No behavior below has
been observed in Positron.** The documentation claims come from Posit pages
read through a web fetch and carry ⚠️ on [the references page](references.qmd).
Two settings files from this group were read on disk and carry ✅, and they
have already corrected this document twice. Section 12 lists the nine checks
outstanding, three of which take about ten minutes each and decide whether the
recommendation in Section 3 does what it says. The finding in Section 5 is the
one to read first.
:::

## 1. Scope

One file, `.posit/assistant/settings.json`, committed to a project
repository, that does two things. It lets the assistant work in the repository
without a confirmation click on every edit. It stops the assistant from
sending patient data to a model provider, and from rewriting shared history.

The reader is a statistician or pharmacometrician using Positron with the
assistant turned on. Agent permission systems are explained from zero in
Section 4. The software developers in the group can start at Section 6.

**Out of scope.** This document does not compare models or providers, does not
cover prompting, and does not cover Posit Workbench administration. It also
does not make the assistant safe to point at identifiable patient data.
Section 10 says why no settings file can do that.

## 2. Positron Assistant Is Now Called Posit Assistant

The product was renamed, and both names are in circulation.

| Version | Name | Setting that turns it on |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.04 | Positron Assistant, in preview | `positron.assistant.enable` |
| 2026.07 and later | Posit Assistant, on by default | `assistant.enabled`, gated by `ai.enabled` |

Posit Assistant is Positron Assistant and Databot merged into one product. The
older `positron.assistant.enable` setting is legacy and applies only before
2026.07. Documentation written against the older name still describes the
current product in most respects, and the configuration file described in
Section 6 is new with the rename.

## 3. The Recommendation

Set the approval mode to `auto`, allow `executeCode`, and write nothing else.

```json
{
  "approvalMode": "auto",
  "permission": {
    "executeCode": "allow"
  }
}
```

The second line is there because `executeCode` runs R or Python in the active
console session, which is the tool this group uses most. Section 4 says why no
`bash` rule constrains it.

The file is short because of the question in Section 3.1, which is the one to
ask before writing any rule at all.

### 3.1 Ask What Git Cannot Undo

A permission rule earns its place only if it prevents something a `git restore`
or a `git checkout` cannot. Sorting the risks that way empties most of the file.

**Git undoes it, so no rule is needed.** A file deleted, overwritten,
mangled or half-rewritten inside the project. A model definition changed by
mistake. A lock file or a dependency list edited as a side effect of other
work. All of these are recoverable from the last commit, and the cost of the
mistake is the time since that commit.

**Git does not undo it, and `auto` already covers it.** Anything outside the
working directory, which is the boundary the mode is defined by. Credentials
sent to an external endpoint. A force-push. A remote script piped into an
interpreter. These are on Posit's published list of what the classifier blocks.

**Git does not undo it, and nothing here covers it.** Data sent to the model
provider, which Section 5 is about, and which no permission rule addresses.

The second group is the only one where a written rule would add anything, and
`auto` is already handling it. That is why the file is two settings.

### 3.2 Commit Often, Because That Is the Actual Control

The recommendation above rests on git, so the habit has to be real. Everything
inside the project is recoverable to the last commit and nothing before it.
Uncommitted work is the only project material that a mistake can destroy
permanently, and it is the one thing no setting in this document protects.

An assistant working in `auto` mode moves faster than one asking permission,
which means more changes between commits unless the commits get more frequent.
The mode and the habit go together.

### 3.3 What You Might Add Later, and Why You Probably Will Not

Three rules were in an earlier draft of this recommendation and came out. Each
is listed with what it would buy, in case a project turns up that needs it.

`"bash": {"git push --force*": "deny"}` duplicates a block `auto` already
performs. It is written down rather than left to a classifier, which is the
only argument for it. Add it if you push to a branch other people build on.

`"external_directory": "ask"` duplicates the working-directory boundary that
defines `auto`. Add it if you often open a workspace whose root is wider than
one project, such as a folder containing every repository you have.

`"bash": {"rm -rf *": "deny"}` is discussed in Section 8.4. The short version
is that it guards the case git already covers, and misses the spelling
variants.

**⚠️ One thing here is unverified.** Whether `approvalMode` is accepted in a
project-level settings file, or only globally. Section 12 has the check, and it
takes about a minute.

## 4. How an Agent Permission System Decides What to Do

The assistant does not edit a file or run a command directly. It proposes a
**tool call**, which is a named request such as "edit `model.R`" or "run
`quarto render`". A permission layer sits between the proposal and the action
and returns one of three answers.

- `allow` runs the tool call with no prompt.
- `ask` shows the proposal and waits for a click.
- `deny` refuses the tool call and tells the assistant it was refused.

Each tool has a key used in the settings file. The reference page gives
examples for four of them, and the full set is longer. These are the ones that
decide anything here.

| Key | What it governs | Why it is in this table |
|---|---|---|
| `executeCode` | Running R or Python in the active console session | The tool this group uses most, and the one Section 10 is about |
| `bash` | Shell commands, matched as patterns | Where `git` and file manipulation rules go |
| `edit` | Changing or creating a file, matched per file pattern | Items 2, 3 and 11 of the checklist |
| `read` | Reading a file | Everything an assistant does starts here |
| `external_directory` | Any path outside the working directory | The boundary `auto` mode is defined against |
| `webfetch` | Retrieving a URL, including an intranet address | Section 5 |
| `task` | Spawning a subagent, by type | Subtypes `explore` and `general` |
| `skill` | Invoking a named skill | Appears in real configurations in this group |

The remaining documented keys are `glob`, `grep`, `list`, `websearch`,
`todowrite`, `question`, `lsp` and `doom_loop`. None needs a rule in a
pharmacometrics project.

Both `bash` and `edit` take patterns rather than a single answer, so
`"git *": "allow"` and `"rm *": "deny"` can sit side by side, and so can
`"*.R": "allow"` and `"renv.lock": "ask"`. A tool can also take one answer for
everything it does, written as `"read": "allow"`.

Two things then decide the answer to a given tool call. The per-tool rules in
the settings file answer the calls they match. The **approval mode** is the
posture that answers everything the rules do not mention, and Section 8
compares the four modes available.

A configuration is working when a prompt appears for actions that leave the
repository, and for nothing else. Prompting on every file edit is the
complaint that started this project. Never prompting at all has its own
section, Section 10.

## 5. What the Assistant Sends Without Being Asked

Posit Assistant attaches context to a chat turn automatically, and the list
includes the contents of the R or Python session.

- The file open in the active editor.
- The console history, both the code entered and the output it printed.
- The in-memory objects and data frames shown in the Variables pane.
- The current plot.
- The project structure and its version control history.

The setting `assistant.aiExcludes` takes a list of glob patterns, in the style
of a `.gitignore` file, and excludes matching **files** from inline completions
and chat context.

**⚠️ Excluding a data file may not exclude the data.** The documentation
describes `aiExcludes` as operating on file contents, and describes the
Variables pane as a separate context source. Read literally, a data frame read
from an excluded CSV file still reaches the provider through the session
context once it is in memory. This has not been tested and it is the first
thing to check.

**❌ Do not point the assistant at a session holding identifiable patient data
until that check is done.** A settings file is the wrong control for this
problem in any case. De-identify before the data reaches the machine, and keep
the assistant off any project where that has not happened.

## 6. Where the Settings Live, and Which File Wins

Posit Assistant reads a plain JSON file at two levels.

| Level | Path | Committed to the repository |
|---|---|---|
| Global, all projects | `~/.posit/assistant/settings.json` | No |
| Project | `.posit/assistant/settings.json` in the project root | Yes |

Both paths were confirmed on disk on 2026-09-12 rather than taken from the
documentation. The project file is where the Positron approval dialog writes a
permission granted with the "For this project" scope, and it is tracked in git
in the projects in this group that have one.

Settings resolve last-wins in this order: built-in defaults, then the global
file, then the project file, then environment variables, then command-line
flags. A project file therefore overrides a personal one, which is the
behavior wanted here. The project file is checked in so that everyone working
in the repository gets the same posture.

Model provider connections are a separate global file, `~/.posit/ai/providers.json`,
and are not part of this project. Credentials do not belong in a committed
file.

Two environment variables are available to whoever administers a shared
Workbench: `POSIT_ASSISTANT_SETTINGS_ENFORCED` sits above everything and
cannot be overridden, and `POSIT_ASSISTANT_SETTINGS_DEFAULT` sits below
everything. An enforced `approvalMode` acts as a ceiling rather than a fixed
value, so a user can still choose a stricter mode than the administrator set.

## 7. The Feature Checklist

Each row is a behavior, a verdict, and the setting that implements it. The
verdict reads: ✅ runs with no prompt, ⚠️ prompts for a click, ❌ refused.

### 7.1 Reading and Editing in the Repository

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Implemented by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Read any file in the project | ✅ | `"read": "allow"` |
| 2 | Edit an existing file in the project | ✅ | `"edit": "allow"` |
| 3 | Create a new file in the project | ✅ | `"edit": "allow"` |
| 4 | Delete a file | ⚠️ | `"rm *": "ask"` |
| 5 | Write anywhere outside the project | ❌ | `sandbox.enabled`, Section 9 |
| 6 | Read `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, other credential paths | ❌ | `sandbox.enabled`, Section 9 |

Items 1 to 3 are the point of the exercise. An agent that asks permission to
edit the file it was asked to edit is slower than doing the work by hand, and
the group's complaint about the default is exactly this.

### 7.2 Running Code

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Implemented by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Run R or Python in the console session | ✅ | `"executeCode": "allow"` |
| 7a | Run an R or Python script from the shell | ✅ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 8 | Render a Quarto document | ✅ | `"quarto *": "allow"` |
| 9 | Run a test suite | ✅ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 10 | Install a package | ✅ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 11 | Modify a dependency or model definition file | ✅ | `approvalMode: auto`, and see below |
| 12 | Submit a job to a cluster or remote host | ❌ | `"ssh *": "deny"`, `"sbatch *": "deny"` |

Items 10 and 11 were ⚠️ in an earlier draft, on a reproducibility argument: a
lock file or a model definition changed as a side effect of other work is a
change nobody reviewed. Both are ✅ now. The change is recorded in Section 11,
and the reason is the test in Section 3.1. A dependency list or an `.mlxtran`
model file that changes by mistake is recoverable from the last commit, so a
prompt buys a review that the diff already provides.

Item 7 is the one to get right for this group. Posit Assistant has built-in
access to the active R or Python session and can run code in it without any
configuration. The `executeCode` tool is how, and Section 10 explains what it
does to every other rule in the file.

Item 12 is more of a concern here than in general software work. A model fit
that takes four hours on a cluster is expensive to start by accident, and the
cost lands on a shared queue.

### 7.3 Version Control

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Implemented by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | `git status`, `git diff`, `git log` | ✅ | `"git *": "allow"` |
| 14 | `git add`, `git commit` on the current branch | ✅ | `"git *": "allow"` |
| 15 | `git push` | ⚠️ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 16 | `git push --force` | ❌ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 17 | `git reset --hard`, `git checkout` over local changes | ⚠️ | `approvalMode: auto` |

Committing freely and pushing on a prompt is the split that fits the way this
group works. A commit is local and reversible. A push is visible to everyone
and, in the force case, destroys work that is not yours.

All three rows are handled by the mode rather than by a written rule. `auto`
allows committing to the current branch and blocks force-pushing by name.
Section 3.3 gives the argument for writing the force rule down anyway, and the
argument for not bothering.

### 7.4 The Outside World

| # | Behavior | Verdict | Implemented by |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 | Read-only web requests for documentation | ✅ | `approvalMode: auto` |
| 19 | Send file contents to the model provider | ⚠️ | `assistant.aiExcludes`, Section 5 |
| 20 | Send session variables to the model provider | ❌ | not solvable in settings, Section 5 |
| 21 | Spawn a subagent | ⚠️ | `"task": {"general": "ask"}` |
| 22 | Run an MCP server not listed in the project file | ❌ | `mcpServers`, unset by default |

Model Context Protocol, abbreviated MCP, is a way of giving an assistant extra
tools from an external process. An MCP server can do anything its author wrote
it to do, and it is outside every rule in this file. None is configured here.

### 7.5 Converting a Configuration Built by Clicking

The Positron approval dialog writes each granted permission into
`.posit/assistant/settings.json`. Clicking through a few weeks of work produces
a file of thirty or forty entries that nobody chose as a set. Two real examples
from this group were read on 2026-09-12, and the same three things were true of
both.

**Most entries are redundant under `auto`.** Rules for `git status`,
`git diff`, `git log`, `git add`, `git commit`, `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`,
`ls`, `cp`, `R`, `Rscript`, `quarto render`, reading files, and fetching public
documentation are all inside the working directory or read-only. The mode
covers them. They can be deleted.

**Four kinds of entry survive the conversion.** Pushing to a remote, reaching
outside the project directory, running code in the console session, and
fetching an internal address. Section 3 has a rule for each of the first three.

**Neither file contained a single `deny`.** A configuration assembled by
clicking Allow can only ever be an allowlist, because the dialog is only asked
when something is about to run. Nothing accumulated that way will ever block a
force-push or a credential read. The denials have to be written by hand, once.

Two specific entries to look for when converting a file.

⚠️ **`"bash": {"*": "allow"}`** makes every other `bash` entry in the file
decorative. Whether it also overrides a later `deny` is open question 4.

⚠️ **`"git push *": "allow"`** appears to match `git push --force` as well,
since the force flag is part of the argument string the pattern globs over.
That is open question 5, and until it is answered a separate `deny` on the
force case is the safe way to write it.

## 8. The Approval Modes

Four modes, ordered from most to least restrictive.

| Mode | What it does | Claude Code equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| `restricted` | Confirmation on every action. Blocks project memory files and subagents. Applied automatically to an untrusted workspace | Plan mode, roughly |
| `normal` | Safe operations run, risky ones prompt. Approvals can be granted once, for the session, or for the project. The default | Default mode |
| `auto` | A classifier model judges each risky tool call. Actions inside the working directory run. A fixed list of operations is blocked | Auto |
| `yolo` | Everything except explicitly dangerous operations runs with no prompt | `--dangerously-skip-permissions` |

The choice in practice is between `normal` and `auto`, and Sections 8.1 to 8.3
are about that choice. `restricted` is for a repository you did not write and
do not trust. `yolo` removes the classifier that makes `auto` acceptable, and
Section 10 is the argument against it.

### 8.1 What Each Mode Does Differently

The modes differ in who decides a risky call, and in what happens to the
decision afterwards. The second difference is the one that changes how a
project looks after two months.

| | `normal` | `auto` |
|---|---|---|
| Who judges a risky tool call | You, in a dialog box | A classifier model reading the call |
| What the judgment is based on | A fixed classification of operations into safe and risky | The command, the path it touches, and the context it was requested in |
| Where the boundary sits | Wherever your accumulated approvals have put it | The working directory, plus a fixed blocked list |
| Is the decision written down | Yes, if you choose "for this project" | No |
| Prompts per hour | Many at first, fewer over time | Few, and the number does not drift |
| What a mistake costs | A permanent allowlist entry made while thinking about something else | One misjudged call, not persisted |

**`auto` allows what stays inside the working directory.** Reading and editing
files, running tests and builds, committing to the current branch, and
read-only web requests. **It blocks a published list:** piping a remote script
into an interpreter, sending credentials to an external endpoint, force-pushing,
and modifying production infrastructure.

`normal` has no equivalent published list. It classifies operations as safe or
risky and prompts on the risky ones, and the documentation does not enumerate
which is which.

### 8.2 Normal Gets Looser Over Time and Auto Does Not

The dialog box in `normal` offers three scopes: allow once, allow for this
session, allow for this project. The third writes a permanent entry into
`.posit/assistant/settings.json`.

That is where the two configurations in Section 7.5 came from. Neither was
designed. Both are the residue of clicking the third button while thinking
about the analysis rather than about the permission. One of them contains
`"bash": {"*": "allow"}`, which permits every shell command in that project
from then on, and which nobody would write deliberately.

So the two modes cross over.

- On day one, `normal` is stricter. It prompts on things `auto` would run.
- On day sixty, `normal` is looser. Its boundary has moved to wherever the
  accumulated approvals put it, and it only ever moves outward. The boundary in
  `auto` on day sixty is the boundary on day one.

A dialog that appears many times a day also stops being read. The prompts in
`normal` are frequent enough to become a reflex, and a reflex is not a review.
Blocks in `auto` are rare enough to be informative when they happen.

**✅ `auto` is the recommendation, and the accumulation argument is the
stronger half of the reason.** The weaker half is that it prompts less, which
is what makes people ask for it.

### 8.3 The Demotion, and Why Normal Is the Floor

If the classifier blocks three tool calls in a row, the session drops back to
`normal` and starts prompting again. A session that suddenly asks permission
for everything has not broken. It has been demoted, and the thing to look at is
what the assistant was trying to do when it was blocked.

`normal` is therefore the floor of `auto` rather than an alternative to it.
Choosing `auto` is choosing where the session starts, not a promise about where
it stays.

### 8.4 Neither Mode Documents What It Does With `rm -rf`

The obvious expectation is that any mode catches a recursive delete. Neither
mode's documentation says so.

`auto` publishes what it blocks, and deletion is not on the list. A `rm -rf` on
a path inside the working directory is inside the boundary the mode allows. A
`rm -rf` on a path outside it crosses the boundary and is gated for that
reason, not because of what the command is.

`normal` would presumably classify a recursive delete as risky and prompt. That
is an inference from the phrase "safe operations run automatically", not a
documented behavior, and it holds only until someone clicks "for this project"
on an `rm` command once.

**A written `deny` beats both.** The documentation states that a deny rule is
absolute, that no approval, mode or setting gets past it, and that deny rules
are enforced even in `auto` and `yolo`. So `"rm -rf *": "deny"` does what it
says.

Two reasons it is still not in the recommendation.

It guards the case git already covers. A recursive delete inside the project is
recoverable from the last commit, and a recursive delete outside the project is
already gated by the working-directory boundary.

It matches a spelling rather than an intent. `rm -rf build` matches the
pattern. `rm -fr build`, `rm -r -f build` and `rm --recursive --force build` are
different strings, and `unlink("build", recursive = TRUE)` in the R console is
not a `bash` call at all. A rule that catches one spelling of four, on a case
git already covers, buys less than it appears to.

## 9. The Sandbox

Setting `sandbox.enabled` to `true` runs shell commands inside an
operating-system sandbox. On macOS it uses Seatbelt, on Linux bubblewrap. The
sandbox restricts writes to the workspace and temporary directories, blocks
network access, and prevents reading paths such as `~/.ssh` and `~/.aws`. On
Windows the same setting turns on a gated mode that checks commands against a
built-in allowlist.

**⚠️ Turning the sandbox on breaks package installation.** Blocking network
access from shell commands stops `install.packages()`, `renv::restore()`, and
`pip install` when the assistant runs them. For a project whose dependencies
are already restored, that is a fair trade and the sandbox should be on. For a
project being set up, it is not, and the choice has to be made per project
rather than once for the group.

The sandbox is the only item in this document that enforces items 5 and 6 of
the checklist by a mechanism outside the assistant. Everything else depends on
the assistant honoring its own configuration.

## 10. What a Settings File Cannot Do

Both vendors state the same caution, and it should be quoted rather than
paraphrased in a group where some readers will assume otherwise. Posit
describes these controls as best-effort administrative policy and not a
security boundary, noting that a user who controls their own environment can
reach a provider directly whatever the settings say. The VS Code documentation,
which covers the chat interface Positron inherits, says terminal auto-approval
is a best-effort convenience and not a security boundary, because command
detection varies across shells and an obfuscated command can evade a pattern.

Three consequences follow for this group.

**`executeCode` is a way around every `bash` rule in the file.** R's `system()`
and `system2()`, and Python's `subprocess`, run any shell command. A carefully
written `bash` allowlist sitting beside `"executeCode": {"*": "allow"}`
constrains the assistant only as long as the assistant chooses the shell rather
than the console. Posit's own extension documentation says to treat
`executeCode` with caution for this reason, because R and Python both run
arbitrary code with the user's full permissions.

The consequence is not that `executeCode` should be denied. Denying it removes
the reason to use Posit Assistant over a general coding agent. The consequence
is that `bash` rules are a guard against the assistant doing something careless
by the obvious route, and they should be read as no stronger than that.

A pattern such as `"rm *": "deny"` guards against an accident. It does not
guard against an adversary, because `rm` invoked through a shell variable, a
script, or an R `system()` call never matches the pattern in the first place.

The classifier in `auto` mode is one model judging another model's request. It
lowers the accident rate. It proves nothing.

Confidentiality of patient data is handled before Positron opens, by
de-identification and by which machine the data sits on. No value in this file
substitutes for that.

## 11. What Was Considered and Rejected

**A rule protecting `renv.lock`. Rejected, reinstated, then rejected again.**
An early draft argued that `edit` takes one answer for every file, so
protecting a single file meant reintroducing the prompt-on-every-edit problem.
That was wrong, and real configurations in this group settle it: entries such
as `"*.R": "allow"` show the key takes a pattern per file. The rule went into
the recommendation on 2026-09-12 and came out the same day, for a better
reason than the first one. No project in this group uses renv, and a lock file
that changes by mistake is recoverable from the last commit. The rule protected
a file that does not exist against a loss that git already covers.

**The same rule applied to `.mlxtran` model definitions.** Proposed as the live
version of the reproducibility concern, since Monolix model files are edited in
these projects and a lock file is not. Rejected by Andy on 2026-09-12: creating
and editing model files is ordinary work and should not prompt, and a mistake is
recoverable from version control. This is the case that produced the test in
Section 3.1, which then removed two further rules.

**`"rm -rf *": "deny"`.** Kept for one turn on the grounds that a written deny
beats any mode. Removed because it guards the case git already covers and
matches one spelling out of several. Section 8.4 has the argument.

**`yolo` as the default.** It matches the request to have the assistant work
freely, and it removes the classifier that makes `auto` acceptable in a
repository holding analysis code. The three-block demotion in `auto` is a
feature for this reason.

**Putting the settings in `.vscode/settings.json`.** Positron is built on VS
Code and reads that file, but the assistant's permission vocabulary is Posit's
own and lives in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`. The VS Code chat settings
such as `chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove` belong to GitHub Copilot Chat. Which
of the two applies when both are present is an open question, recorded below.

## 12. Open Questions

1. **Is `approvalMode` accepted in a project-level file?** The documentation
   lists the per-project settings explicitly, and `approvalMode` is not among
   them. It appears in the section on administrator environment variables.
   Section 3 depends on the answer. Check by setting it in a project file and
   reading the mode indicator in the chat pane.
2. **Does `aiExcludes` cover the Variables pane?** Section 5 says it does not,
   read literally. Check by loading an excluded CSV file into a data frame and
   asking the assistant what columns it has.
3. **Does the `auto` classifier gate `executeCode` at all?** The mode is
   described in terms of the working directory, and a console session has no
   directory. If the classifier does not see console code, `auto` constrains
   less than Section 8 claims.
4. **Inside one tool block, does a specific pattern beat `*`?** A file
   containing both `"*": "allow"` and `"rm *": "deny"` under `bash` behaves
   very differently depending on the answer. The documentation gives the
   resolution order across files and says nothing about within one. Partly
   closed on 2026-09-12: a `deny` is documented as absolute and enforced even
   in `auto` and `yolo`, so a deny beats an allow. Whether a specific `allow`
   beats a general one is still open.
5. **Does `git push*` match `git push --force`?** Relevant only to anyone
   adding the optional rule in Section 3.3.
6. **Does the sandbox cover `executeCode`?** The sandbox is documented as
   sandboxing shell tool execution. If console code is outside it, then
   `system()` in R escapes the sandbox as well as the `bash` rules, and
   Section 9 claims more than it should.
7. **What is the exact key for `aiExcludes` after the rename?** The
   documentation shows `positron.assistant.aiExcludes` in the 2026.02 release
   notes and `assistant.aiExcludes` in the current settings table.
8. **Do the VS Code chat settings apply at the same time?** If
   `chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove` is also read, a project needs consistent
   rules in two files.
9. **What does the `auto` classifier do with a long-running R script?** A
   four-hour model fit inside the working directory is not risky by the
   classifier's definition and is expensive by ours.

Questions 1, 4 and 5 are each answerable in about ten minutes at a Positron
prompt, and together they decide whether the file in Section 3 does what it
says.

## 13. Where to Start

For the reader who wants to use this today, in order.

1. Read Section 5, then decide whether the project has data that cannot go to
   a provider. If it does, stop and fix that first.
2. Copy the file in Section 3 into `.posit/assistant/settings.json` and commit
   it.
3. Delete whatever the approval dialog has already accumulated in that file.
   Section 7.5 says how to tell which entries are worth keeping, and the answer
   is usually none of them.
4. Work for a week, committing often. Section 3.2 is the reason the habit
   carries the configuration.
5. Add a rule only when a specific prompt has annoyed you twice, or when
   something happened that git could not undo. Section 3.3 lists the three
   candidates and the argument against each.

For the reader deciding whether to adopt any of this, read Sections 3.1, 8.2
and 10. They are the test that empties the settings file, the reason `auto`
beats `normal` over time, and the limit of what any of it buys.
